rows.name: floating-counterexample
rows.question: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.answer:
For the original triple, both parenthesizations give 1. For the changed triple, the left-parenthesized expression gives 0, while the right-parenthesized expression gives 1, assuming IEEE binary32’s default round-to-nearest, ties-to-even mode.

Binary32 has 24 bits of significand precision. All integers from −16777216 through +16777216 are exactly representable. Immediately above +16777216, representable numbers are spaced 2 apart; immediately below it, they are spaced 1 apart.

Original triple:
• (16777216 + −16777216) + 1: the first addition cancels exactly to 0, and 0 + 1 is exactly 1.
• 16777216 + (−16777216 + 1): the inner result is −16777215, which is exactly representable. Adding 16777216 then gives exactly 1. Neither parenthesization incurs a rounding error.

Changed triple:
• (16777216 + 1) + −16777216: the exact first sum is 16777217, which is not representable. It lies halfway between 16777216 and 16777218; ties-to-even rounds it to 16777216. The final addition therefore cancels exactly to 0.
• 16777216 + (1 + −16777216): the inner result is −16777215, which is exactly representable, and the final addition gives exactly 1.

So the difference comes specifically from rounding the positive intermediate sum 16777217—not from the negative intermediate sum −16777215, which is representable. If a different IEEE rounding mode is intended, that mode must be specified because it can change the rounded result.

review.note: Actualoriginal1/1 and changed0/1; ties-even assumption disclosed, 16777217 midpoint and -16777215 exact, spacing around2^24 explained.
review.usefulPrefix: For the original triple, both parenthesizations give 1. For the changed triple, the left-parenthesized expression gives 0, while the right-parenthesized expression gives 1, assuming IEEE binary32’s default round-to-nearest, ties-to-even mode.

rows.name: quorum-counterexample
rows.question: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.answer:
Without read write-back, the protocol is not linearizable: a read can expose an incomplete write, then a later read can return the older version. Writing the selected version back to three replicas before returning fixes this counterexample by making every completed read’s version visible to every subsequent read quorum.

Here is a fully ordered execution. Denote each replica’s stored version by a five-tuple in A,B,C,D,E order, and start with (0,0,0,0,0).

1. The writer invokes W to write version 1.
2. A receives version 1, stores it, and acknowledges. Delay delivery to all other replicas. The state is (1,0,0,0,0); W has only one acknowledgement and remains incomplete.
3. Reader R1 is invoked and queries A,B,C. Their replies are 1,0,0. R1 returns version 1 without write-back. The state remains (1,0,0,0,0).
4. Only after R1 returns, reader R2 is invoked and queries B,C,D. Their replies are 0,0,0. R2 returns version 0. The state is still (1,0,0,0,0), and W is still incomplete.

For the attempted linearization, R1’s return of 1 forces the pending write W to be included and ordered before R1: no other operation wrote version 1. Because R1 finishes before R2 starts, real-time order requires R1 before R2. Thus the sequential order must contain W < R1 < R2, but with no intervening write, R2 must return 1 rather than 0. Omitting W instead makes R1’s return impossible. Therefore no legal linearization exists—even though both reads overlap the incomplete write.

Now change the reader to write its selected version to three replicas and wait for all three acknowledgements before returning. In the same execution, suppose R1 writes version 1 to A,B,C. Before R1 returns, the state becomes (1,1,1,0,0). R2 querying B,C,D now receives 1,1,0 and returns 1.

This does not depend on which three replicas acknowledge R1’s write-back. Any set of three replicas intersects any other set of three among five replicas, since 3 + 3 > 5. At least one replica in R2’s query quorum therefore retains version 1 or higher; replicas never decrease their stored versions. Consequently, R2 cannot return version 0, and the counterexample is eliminated. A read that exposes an incomplete write effectively makes that version durable on a quorum before completing.

For a full linearizable-register guarantee, the version-generation assumptions also matter. With a single writer assigning increasing versions, and acknowledgements confirming storage of that version or a higher one, this read-write-back protocol provides the standard quorum-register guarantee. With multiple writers, quorum write-back alone is not a complete specification: writers also need a suitable protocol for generating unique, totally ordered versions consistent with real-time write order.

review.note: ActualpendingA-onlywrite1, R1ABCreturns1 before R2BCDreturns0. PendingWmustbeincluded W<R1<R2 or R1unexplained. Read write-back quorum intersection repairs counterexample; full guarantee qualified single-writer/version allocation.
review.usefulPrefix: Without read write-back, the protocol is not linearizable: a read can expose an incomplete write, then a later read can return the older version. Writing the selected version back to three replicas before returning fixes this counterexample by making every completed read’s version visible to every subsequent read quorum.

rows.name: quorum-why
rows.question: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.answer:
Because linearizability must explain completed reads in one sequential register history, even when the write they observed never finished. If the first read R1 returns the new value v1 and completes before the second read R2 is invoked, real-time order requires R1 before R2.

Assuming the initial value is v0 and the only write W writes v1, explaining R1’s result requires including the pending W in the linearized history and placing it before R1. Thus the order must be W before R1 before R2; with no intervening write, R2 must also return v1. Returning v0 creates the contradiction.

This does not require every unfinished operation to complete in the actual execution. Linearizability permits pending operations to be omitted or supplied with hypothetical responses when constructing a legal history, but W cannot be omitted here because then R1’s returned value would have no explanation.

review.note: Completed R1 before R2 start imposes real-time order; explaining observed1 includes pendingWbeforeR1. Hypothetical completion/omission does not require every unfinished operation to finish.

rows.name: backend-reconnection
rows.question: Why must desired be recomputed after that failure? Refer to the concrete values in the preceding explanation, and state what is retained across a reconnection.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why must desired be recomputed after that failure? Refer to the concrete values in the preceding explanation, and state what is retained across a reconnection.
rows.answer:
Because a failed compare_exchange_weak updates expected, but does not update desired: the next increment must be computed from the newly observed value. For a concrete example, suppose expected was 0 and desired was 1; another thread increments the counter to 1, so your CAS fails and updates expected to 1. Retrying with the stale desired of 1 can then successfully replace 1 with 1, losing your increment; recomputing desired as expected + 1 makes it 2 instead. A spurious failure also requires retrying, with desired recomputed from whatever expected contains after the failure.

Across a retry, the local variables are retained: expected contains the value supplied by the failed CAS, while desired retains its old value unless explicitly reassigned. If you literally mean a reconnection rather than a retry, this C++ code specifies no reconnection or persistence behavior; what survives would depend on whether the same process and operation remain alive.
